prime.problem: Training gave you a list of merges and a model will give you a list of ids, but people read text. Without a decoder you can't see what the model said, and a naive decoder crashes the first time the model emits bytes that aren't valid UTF-8.
prime.fits: The training loop minted ids 256–275 as pairs of older ids. This card turns that merge table into vocab (id → bytes) and uses the UTF-8 rules from the code points card to explain when bytes are, and aren't, text.
prime.goal: Write decode, explain why decode([128]) fails while decode([263, 153]) works, and choose between strict, replace, ignore and streaming decoding.

attend: Why can vocab be built in a single pass over merges, and what would break if the dict lost its insertion order?
Byte 128 is a perfectly good vocab entry. What exactly about 10000000 makes it invalid as the first byte of text?
Why must the bytes of all tokens be joined before calling .decode, rather than decoding token by token?
Nothing stops a model from sampling [128]. What does that say about where a � in LLM output comes from?
What information does errors="replace" throw away, and which later operation notices the loss?

must: each merged id = its two parents' bytes concatenated → built in merge order, both parents already exist → one pass over merges gives every id's bytes (vocab[275] = b'th' + b'e ' = b'the ')
tokens are byte runs, not characters → a character can be split across tokens (’ = 263 + 153) → join all bytes first, then decode once, or split characters turn into �

the model picks any id at every step → nothing forces valid UTF-8 → a lone continuation byte like 128 (10xxxxxx) or a cut-off emoji can appear → strict decode raises UnicodeDecodeError, so use errors="replace" and show �
replace maps many different bad byte runs to the same � → decode is lossy on invalid input → encode(decode(ids)) can't recover the ids ([128] comes back as [239, 191, 189])
elevated: Half the base ids are fragments: all 128 bytes ≥ 128 fail to decode alone, and a learned merge can be a fragment too (263 = e2 80) → 129 of the 276 ids can't be printed on their own → streaming output must hold back bytes until a character completes (an incremental decoder)
reference: vocab = {idx: bytes([idx]) for idx in range(256)}, then vocab[idx] = vocab[p0] + vocab[p1]
Python dicts keep insertion order since 3.7
byte ranges: 0–127 ASCII, 128–191 continuation, 194–244 lead, 192, 193 and 245–255 never valid
minbpe basic.py L51–L55 and base.py _build_vocab; GPT-2 encoder.py also uses errors='replace'

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the decode pipeline for [104, 105, 256, 275] and for [128]: ids → bytes → text. Mark the one place it can fail and say in 2–3 sentences why it fails and what errors="replace" changes.
checklist: vocab is built from merges in order: base bytes, then each child = parent bytes + parent bytes
decode = look up every id, join all the bytes, decode as UTF-8 once
failure point: the bytes aren't valid UTF-8 (128 = 10000000 is a continuation byte with no lead byte)
the model can emit any id sequence, so this isn't a rare bug
replace turns bad bytes into � instead of crashing, at the cost of losing the exact bytes

retrieve.q: Explain why a byte-level vocab can contain tokens that are not text at all, using one base id and one learned id as examples.
answer: tokens are byte runs chosen by frequency, not characters
base id 128 is a lone continuation byte
learned id 263 is e2 80, the first two bytes of ’ “ ”
they only become text next to the right neighbouring bytes

retrieve.q: Walk through decode([104, 105, 256, 275]): what does each lookup return, what is the joined byte string, and what comes out?
answer: b'h', b'i', b'e ', b'the '
joined: b'hie the ' (8 bytes)
decoded: 'hie the '

retrieve.q: Walk through what happens in a strict decode of [240, 159], and then with errors="replace".
answer: 240 is a 4-byte lead byte, 159 a continuation
the bytes end after 2 of the 4 the lead byte promised
strict: UnicodeDecodeError; replace: one '�'

retrieve.q: You're building a chat UI that prints tokens as they are sampled. Compare strict decode, errors="ignore", per-token replace, and an incremental decoder. Which do you ship, and what does each cost?
answer: strict: crashes on the first bad sample
ignore: never crashes, but silently deletes bytes, so garbage goes unnoticed
per-token replace: splits multi-byte characters (👋 in two tokens → '���')
incremental decoder with replace: holds back an unfinished character and prints it whole, and still shows � for truly bad bytes

compare.q: The GPT lecture's decode was ''.join(itos[i] for i in l) and could never fail. What design choice made it safe, what did that choice cost, and why did byte-level BPE give it up?
answer: each id there is a whole character, so any sequence of ids is valid text
cost: only the 65 characters seen in Shakespeare, so any other character can't be encoded at all
byte-level BPE can encode any string, but its ids are byte runs that can form invalid UTF-8, so decode needs a fallback

compare.q: Decode and encode are inverses on paper. Which round trip always holds, which one doesn't, and which property of decode causes the asymmetry?
answer: decode(encode(text)) == text holds for any string, because encode starts from valid UTF-8
encode(decode(ids)) fails for invalid id sequences
cause: replace maps many byte runs to the same �, so decode isn't one-to-one
example: [128] and [240, 159] both come back as [239, 191, 189]

compare.q: sentencepiece works on code points and only falls back to byte tokens like <0xEC> for rare characters. When does its decoder face the same invalid-byte problem as ours, and when can't it?
answer: code-point pieces are whole characters, so they always decode
byte-fallback tokens are UTF-8 fragments, so a model that emits them in a bad order produces invalid bytes
so the trap is limited to the byte-fallback part of the vocab, rather than every id above 127

predict.q: Take decode([240, 159]), the first half of 👋, and feed the resulting string straight into this course's encode. How many ids come back, and are they the ones you started with?
predict.answer: Three ids, [239, 191, 189], not the original two. decode turned the two bytes into one '�' (U+FFFD), and encoding that character gives its own 3 UTF-8 bytes. None of the 20 merges touches them. You get the same three ids back from [128], which shows the information is really gone.

apply.task: Write stream_decode(ids) that returns a list with the text to print after each id, using codecs.getincrementaldecoder('utf-8')(errors='replace') and your vocab. Run it on [104, 105, 263, 153] (h, i, then ’ split across two tokens) and on [240, 159, 145, 139] (👋 as four byte tokens).
apply.done: The first run prints ['h', 'i', '', '’'] and the second ['', '', '', '👋']. For comparison, decoding each id on its own with decode([i]) gives '�' pieces instead.
apply.hint: Create the decoder once, outside the loop, and call d.decode(vocab[i]) for each id. It keeps an unfinished character's bytes until the rest arrive. Call d.decode(b'', final=True) at the end to flush anything left over.
